newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl talks tough on EMU, quiet on own future.
newsitem.headline: Kohl talks tough on EMU, quiet on own future.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl cautioned on Friday his enthusiasm for European integration did not mean he would tolerate any weakening of the Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
But Kohl kept Germans guessing over whether he planned to continue his drive for European unity from the chancellery or might stand down from the top job before the 1998 general election.

"I warn against misunderstanding my commitment to Europe along the lines of 'Kohl is so enthusiastic about Europe that he'll go soft on the stability criteria at the end'," Kohl told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper.
He told Saturday's edition of the paper in an interview released ahead of publication he would guard the tradition of stability, which characterises the deutschemark.

"Anyone who is ready to introduce the euro in place of the mark, as I am, knows that the Germans' experience with the mark is one of the best in history and that we will not give up this accomplishment in the future," the chancellor said.

German political correspondents have gone into overdrive with speculation about Kohl's future this week, some of it fuelled by the chancellor himself after he told French television he had not yet decided if he would stand again.
"As I have said, I will announce my decision punctually at a point in time which I believe to be right," Kohl told the Frankfurter Allgemeine.

He also dismissed speculation that poor health may force him against running again in 1998. The news magazine Der Spiegel -- one of the chancellor's least favourite publications -- has even suggested he has had treatment for a prostate condition.
"I don't have cancer, thank God," Kohl said. "I find that people who work with nasty methods to to bring down a political opponent only damage themselves."
Kohl also spoke out against politicians in one country giving opinions on the chances of another meeting the EMU criteria.
"I am in favour of everyone -- including Germany -- doing their own homework. There's a lot to do. And I'm in favour of the criteria in the (Maastricht) treaty being applied strictly."
